1:1.t: Names follow the spellings already used in Genesis 5, 10, 11, 25 and 36 where they are the same people. The KJV spells Seth, Jared and Enoch as Sheth, Jered and Henoch (1:1-3), Ashkenaz as Ashchenaz (1:6), Sabteca as Sabtecha (1:9), Sidon as Zidon (1:13), and Oholibamah as Aholibamah (1:52).

1:10.t: "The first mighty man": the KJV's "began to be mighty upon the earth".

1:33.t: Hanoch: the KJV spells it Henoch, the same spelling it uses for Enoch in 1:3; Genesis 25:4 has Hanoch.

1:36.t: "Timna, and Amalek": as in the KJV, which lists Timna among the sons of Eliphaz. Genesis 36:12 says Timna was Eliphaz's concubine and the mother of Amalek.

1:39.t: Several names differ slightly from the parallel list in Genesis 36: Homam (Hemam), Alian (Alvan), Shephi (Shepho), Amram (Hemdan; many Hebrew copies read Hamran), Zaavan and Jaakan (the KJV's Zavan and Jakan; Genesis has Zaavan and Akan), Pai (Pau), Hadad (Hadar), Aliah (Alvah). They are kept as the Chronicles text has them.

2:3.t: "A Canaanite woman": the KJV's "the Canaanitess". 2:4 Perez: the KJV spells it Pharez.

2:7.t: Achar: the man called Achan in Joshua 7; his name sounds like akar, "trouble". "What was devoted to destruction": the KJV's "the thing accursed", the Hebrew herem, something handed over entirely to God that could not be kept for personal use. See the Original language note on 2:7.

"Devoted to destruction" (Hebrew herem; verb haram): something under herem was handed over entirely to God, either for the sanctuary or for destruction, and could not be kept for personal use. See Exodus 22:20 and Joshua 6:17. Achar's name sounds like akar, "trouble", the word Joshua used of him (Joshua 7:25).

2:9.t: Chelubai: apparently the same person as Caleb in 2:18 and 2:42.

2:13.t: Shimea and Nethanel: the KJV spells them Shimma and Nethaneel. 2:17 Ishmaelite: the KJV's "Ishmeelite"; 2 Samuel 17:25 calls Jether (Ithra) an Israelite. 2:20 Bezalel: the KJV's Bezaleel.

2:21.t: "Slept with": the KJV's "went in to", meaning married and lived with as husband.

2:23.t: "He took Geshur and Aram ... from them": as in the KJV, with Jair's people as the subject. Many modern Bibles read that Geshur and Aram took the towns of Jair from the Israelites.

2:24.t: Caleb-ephrathah, Abijah, Ashhur: the KJV spells them Caleb-ephratah, Abiah and Ashur. The Greek Old Testament reads "Caleb went in to Ephrathah", the wife of his father Hezron.

2:42.t: Several names here are towns (Ziph, Mareshah, Hebron, Beth-zur, Bethlehem, Kiriath-jearim), so "father of" can mean founder or leader of a town.

2:44.t: Jorkeam: the KJV spells it Jorkoam. 2:40 Sismai: the KJV's Sisamai. 2:48 Maacah: the KJV's Maachah.

2:50.t: "Caleb the son of Hur": the KJV's reading. Since 2:19 makes Hur Caleb's son, many modern Bibles divide the sentence: "These were the descendants of Caleb. The sons of Hur ..."

2:52.t: Manahathites, Puthites, Zorathites, Eshtaolites, Sucathites, Hammath: the KJV spells them Manahethites, Puhites, Zareathites, Eshtaulites, Suchathites and Hemath. 2:54 "Ataroth of the house of Joab": the KJV's "Ataroth, the house of Joab", probably one place name, Atroth-beth-joab.

3:1.t: Daniel: called Chileab in 2 Samuel 3:3. "Of Jezreel", "of Carmel": the KJV's "the Jezreelitess" and "the Carmelitess".

3:5.t: Shimea and Bathshua: 2 Samuel 5:14 has Shammua, and 2 Samuel 11:3 calls Solomon's mother Bathsheba the daughter of Eliam. Ammiel and Eliam are the same name with its parts reversed.

3:10.t: Abijah: the KJV spells it Abia. 3:11 Joram is also called Jehoram. 3:12 Azariah is also called Uzziah.

3:16.t: Jeconiah: also called Jehoiachin and Coniah.

3:17.t: "Assir": as in the KJV, a name. The Hebrew word means "prisoner", so many modern Bibles read "Jeconiah the captive". Shealtiel: the KJV's Salathiel.

3:18.t: Shenazzar, Jekamiah, Jeshaiah, Shecaniah, Igal: the KJV spells them Shenazar, Jecamiah, Jesaiah, Shechaniah and Igeal.

3:21.t: Shenazzar, Jekamiah, Jeshaiah, Shecaniah, Igal: the KJV spells them Shenazar, Jecamiah, Jesaiah, Shechaniah and Igeal.
The line of descent in this verse is unclear in the Hebrew; the Greek Old Testament reads "his son Rephaiah, his son Arnan" and so on.

3:22.t: "Six": only five names are listed, as in the Hebrew.

4:1.t: "Descendants": the KJV's "sons"; these five are successive generations, not brothers.

4:3.t: Hazzelelponi: the KJV spells it Hazelelponi. 4:4 Ephrathah: the KJV's Ephratah. 4:5 Ashhur: the KJV's Ashur. 4:6 Ahuzzam: the KJV's Ahuzam.

4:7.t: Jezoar: as in the KJV's Hebrew text; the Hebrew margin reads Zohar.

4:9.t: Jabez sounds like the Hebrew for "pain" or "sorrow" (otseb), with its letters rearranged.

4:10.t: "Territory": the KJV's "coast", meaning borders or land. "Keep me from harm so that it may not bring me pain": the KJV's "keep me from evil, that it may not grieve me", playing again on the name Jabez.

4:12.t: Recah, Cozeba: the KJV spells them Rechah and Chozeba.

4:22.t: Recah, Cozeba: the KJV spells them Rechah and Chozeba.

4:14.t: "The Valley of Craftsmen": the KJV leaves the Hebrew name untranslated, "the valley of Charashim", and then explains it, "for they were craftsmen".

4:16.t: Jehallelel, Asarel, Ezrah: the KJV spells them Jehaleleel, Asareel and Ezra. 4:18 Soco: the KJV's Socho.

4:17.t: "She bore Miriam": the Hebrew does not say who "she" is. Many modern Bibles move the last sentence of 4:18 up to show that she is Bithiah, Mered's Egyptian wife.

4:18.t: "His Judean wife": the KJV takes the Hebrew as a name, Jehudijah; the word means "the Judean woman".

4:21.t: "The linen workers at Beth-ashbea": the KJV's "the house of them that wrought fine linen, of the house of Ashbea".

4:23.t: "Plantations and walled pens": the KJV's "plants and hedges". The Hebrew words may be place names, Netaim and Gederah.

4:31.t: Beth-biri: the KJV spells it Beth-birei.

4:33.t: "They kept a genealogical record": the KJV's "and their genealogy".

4:41.t: "Destroyed them completely": the Hebrew verb haram is the one used for devoting to destruction, handing something over entirely to God so that nothing was kept for personal use; see 2:7.

"Devoted to destruction" (Hebrew herem; verb haram): something under herem was handed over entirely to God, either for the sanctuary or for destruction, and could not be kept for personal use. See Exodus 22:20 and Joshua 6:17. Achar's name sounds like akar, "trouble", the word Joshua used of him (Joshua 7:25).

5:1.t: "Defiled his father's bed": he slept with his father's concubine Bilhah (Genesis 35:22).

5:2.t: "A ruler": the KJV's "the chief ruler", taken by many as David and his line.

5:5.t: Reaiah: the KJV spells it Reaia. 5:6, 5:26 Tiglath-pileser: the KJV spells it Tilgath-pilneser.

5:9.t: "The Euphrates River": the KJV's "the river Euphrates".

5:10.t: Hagrites: the KJV's "Hagarites", a people of the desert east of Gilead.

5:19.t: Hagrites: the KJV's "Hagarites", a people of the desert east of Gilead.

5:11.t: Salecah, Janai, Jacan, Eber: the KJV spells them Salchah, Jaanai, Jachan and Heber.

5:16.t: "Pasturelands": the KJV's "suburbs", meaning the open land around a town used for grazing. The same word is so rendered throughout chapter 6.

5:18.t: KJV: "four and forty thousand seven hundred and threescore". 5:21 KJV: "an hundred thousand" people, the KJV's "men", taken as captives.

5:20.t: "He answered their prayer": the KJV's "he was intreated of them".

5:25.t: "Prostituted themselves": the KJV's "went a whoring", the Bible's common picture of idolatry as unfaithfulness in marriage.

5:26.t: "Pul ... and Tiglath-pileser": as in the KJV. Pul was another name for Tiglath-pileser III, and the Hebrew "and" can mean "that is"; the verb that follows is singular.

6:1.t: The KJV's chapter 6 matches Hebrew 5:27-6:66, so verse numbers here differ from some modern Bibles, which number 6:1-15 as 5:27-41 (the Hebrew order). The KJV numbering is kept.

6:16.t: Gershom: the same person as Gershon in 6:1.

6:21.t: Jeatherai: the KJV spells it Jeaterai.

6:28.t: "The firstborn Vashni, and Abijah": as in the KJV. 1 Samuel 8:2 names Samuel's firstborn Joel, and the Hebrew vashni can mean "and the second", so many modern Bibles read "Joel the firstborn, and Abijah the second". Abijah: the KJV's Abiah.

6:32.t: "The tabernacle, the tent of meeting": the KJV's "the dwelling place of the tabernacle of the congregation". "Tent of meeting" means the tent where God met with His people.

6:48.t: "The tabernacle, the tent of meeting": the KJV's "the dwelling place of the tabernacle of the congregation". "Tent of meeting" means the tent where God met with His people.

6:33.t: Samuel: the KJV spells it Shemuel here; he is the prophet Samuel (6:28).

6:39.t: "Fellow Levite": the KJV's "brother", meaning kinsman. Berechiah, Malchijah: the KJV's Berachiah and Malchiah. 6:46 Shemer: the KJV's Shamer.

6:49.t: "Most Holy Place": the KJV's "the place most holy", the inner room of the sanctuary. "Make atonement": to remove guilt and defilement so that the relationship with God is restored; see the Original language note on 6:49.

"Make atonement" (Hebrew kaphar): to make atonement means to remove guilt and defilement so that the relationship with God is restored. The root may mean "to cover" or "to wipe clean", and it is related to "ransom" (kopher). See Exodus 29:33.

6:54.t: "Their settlements within their territory": the KJV's "their castles in their coasts". "The first lot": the KJV says only "for theirs was the lot"; Joshua 21:10 says the first lot fell to them.

6:57.t: "The city of refuge": the KJV's "the city of refuge" is singular; Joshua 21 lists Hebron and several others as cities of refuge. 6:67 likewise.

7:2.t: Ibsam: the KJV spells it Jibsam. "Brave warriors": the KJV's "valiant men of might", here and throughout these lists.

7:3.t: Isshiah: the KJV's Ishiah. "Five": four sons are named; the count may include Izrahiah.

7:8.t: Zemirah, Jeremoth, Abijah, Alemeth: the KJV spells them Zemira, Jerimoth, Abiah and Alameth.

7:14.t: Asriel: the KJV's Ashriel. "Aramean concubine": the KJV's "the Aramitess".

7:15.t: "Machir married the sister of Huppim and Shuppim": as in the KJV. The Hebrew is difficult; many modern Bibles read "Machir took a wife for Huppim and Shuppim". "The second": the Hebrew does not say second to whom.

7:18.t: Hammolecheth, Ishhod, Mahlah: the KJV spells them Hammoleketh, Ishod and Mahalah.

7:21.t: "Killed them": the KJV's "slew", referring to Ezer and Elead. "Who were born in the land" means the native people of the region.

7:23.t: "Slept with": the KJV's "went in to". Beriah sounds like the Hebrew for "in disaster" (beraah).

7:24.t: Sheerah, Uzzen-sheerah: the KJV spells them Sherah and Uzzen-sherah. "Lower Beth-horon": the KJV's "Beth-horon the nether".

7:26.t: Ladan, Nun, Joshua: the KJV spells them Laadan, Non and Jehoshua.

7:30.t: Ishvah, Ishvi: the KJV's Isuah and Ishuai; see Genesis 46:17.

7:31.t: Birzaith: the KJV's Birzavith. 7:34 Shemer: the KJV's Shamer, apparently the Shomer of 7:32.

7:38.t: Pispa, Hanniel, Rizia: the KJV spells them Pispah, Haniel and Rezia.

8:1.t: These names differ from the lists in Genesis 46:21 and Numbers 26:38-40, as is common in genealogies that pick out different generations.

8:6.t: The Hebrew of these verses is hard to follow; the KJV's sense is kept.

8:7.t: Ahijah: the KJV's Ahiah. 8:9-10 Malcam, Sachia, Mirmah: the KJV spells them Malcham, Shachia and Mirma.

8:12.t: Shemed, Eder, Ishpah, Hizki, Izliah, Zillethai, Shimei, Eber, Anthothijah, Iphdeiah, Jaareshiah, Elijah: the KJV spells them Shamed, Ader, Ispah, Hezeki, Jezliah, Zilthai, Shimhi, Heber, Antothijah, Iphedeiah, Jaresiah and Eliah.

8:29.t: "The father of Gibeon": 9:35 names him Jeiel. 8:31 Zecher: called Zechariah in 9:37; the KJV spells it Zacher.

8:33.t: Eshbaal: called Ish-bosheth in 2 Samuel 2-4. 8:34 Merib-baal: called Mephibosheth in 2 Samuel. Saul's family used baal, "lord", as a title for the LORD; once Baal had become the name of a Canaanite god, the books of Samuel replaced it with bosheth, "shame". See the Original language note on 8:33-34.

Eshbaal, Merib-baal (Hebrew baal, "lord, master"): baal means "lord", "master" or "owner", and in ordinary Hebrew can mean a husband; as a name it is the Canaanite storm god (see 1 Kings 16:31-32). Saul's family used baal as a title for the LORD, "the Lord's man" and "the Lord contends". Once Baal had become the name of a Canaanite god, the books of Samuel replaced it with bosheth, "shame", giving Ish-bosheth and Mephibosheth. Chronicles keeps the older forms.

8:36.t: Jehoaddah: the KJV's Jehoadah; 9:42 has Jarah. 8:37 Raphah: the KJV's Rapha. 8:39 Jeush: the KJV's Jehush.

9:1.t: "Judah was carried away": the KJV's "who were carried away", which could refer to Israel and Judah together. The Hebrew sets "Judah" at the start of the second sentence.

9:2.t: "Temple servants": the KJV's "Nethinims", from a Hebrew word meaning "those given", people assigned to help the Levites (Ezra 8:20).

9:7.t: Hassenuah, Shephatiah, Pashhur, Maasai, Mica: the KJV spells them Hasenuah, Shephathiah, Pashur, Maasiai and Micah.

9:17.t: "Gatekeepers": the KJV's "porters", meaning those who kept the doors and gates.

9:18.t: "Until now": the KJV's "hitherto", meaning up to the time of writing.

9:19.t: "Thresholds": the KJV's "gates". "The camp of the LORD": the KJV's "the host of the LORD", the camp in the wilderness.

9:21.t: "Tent of meeting": the KJV's "tabernacle of the congregation", the tent where God met with His people; see 6:32.

9:22.t: "Trusted positions", "trusted with the responsibility": the KJV's "set office"; the Hebrew word means faithfulness or trust.

9:26.t: "Trusted positions", "trusted with the responsibility": the KJV's "set office"; the Hebrew word means faithfulness or trust.

9:31.t: "Trusted positions", "trusted with the responsibility": the KJV's "set office"; the Hebrew word means faithfulness or trust.

9:23.t: "Shifts": the KJV's "wards". "Every seven days": the KJV's "after seven days", meaning for a week at a time.

9:25.t: "Shifts": the KJV's "wards". "Every seven days": the KJV's "after seven days", meaning for a week at a time.

9:28.t: "Counted them": the KJV's "by tale", meaning by number.

9:30.t: "Mixed the blend of spices": the KJV's "made the ointment of the spices".

9:32.t: "The bread of the Presence": the KJV's "shewbread", the twelve loaves set out before the LORD each Sabbath (Leviticus 24:5-9). The Hebrew is literally "bread of the face".

9:35.t: Jeiel: the KJV spells it Jehiel. 9:35-44 repeat 8:29-38 with small differences.

10:3.t: "Found him": the KJV's "hit him"; the Hebrew means found or overtook.

10:4.t: "Armor-bearer": the KJV's "armourbearer". "Abuse": the Hebrew can mean to mock or to treat cruelly.

10:13.t: "Medium": the KJV's "one that had a familiar spirit", a person who claimed to call up the dead (1 Samuel 28).

"For guidance", "did not seek guidance" (Hebrew darash): darash means to seek, inquire of, or search out, and it is a key word in Chronicles. To seek the LORD is to turn to Him for guidance and to give Him one's worship and loyalty; to fail to seek Him is the heart of unfaithfulness. Saul sought a medium instead of the LORD, and so lost the kingdom. Through 1 and 2 Chronicles, kings who seek the LORD prosper and those who do not fall. The KJV renders it "enquire", "seek" and "seek unto"; we use "seek" where the meaning is devotion and "consult" or "inquire" where it is a request for an answer.

10:14.t: "The LORD put him to death": the KJV's "he slew him". Saul killed himself (10:4), but the writer sees the hand of God in his death.

11:1.t: "Your own flesh and blood": the KJV's "thy bone and thy flesh".

11:2.t: "Shepherd": the KJV's "feed", in the sense of tending a flock.

11:8.t: "The Millo": a terraced structure or fill in the city of David; the name probably means "filling".

11:9.t: "The LORD of hosts": as in the KJV. The "hosts" are armies, of Israel, the stars and the angels: the title presents the LORD as commander of every power in heaven and on earth. See the Original language note on 11:9.

"The LORD of hosts" (Hebrew YHWH tseva'ot): tseva'ot means armies, and the "hosts" are the armies of Israel, the stars, and the angels of heaven. The title presents the LORD as commander of every power in heaven and on earth. See 1 Samuel 1:3.

11:11.t: "Chief of the officers": the KJV's "chief of the captains"; some Hebrew copies read "chief of the thirty" or "of the three". "300": 2 Samuel 23:8 has 800.

11:20.t: "The three": some Hebrew copies and ancient translations read "the thirty" here, which fits the sense better ("more honored than the thirty").

11:22.t: "Two of Moab's mightiest warriors": the KJV's "two lionlike men of Moab". The Hebrew ariel may mean "lion of God", a title for a great warrior.

11:26.t: Compare 2 Samuel 23:24-39; several names are spelled differently there. Place names are given as "of Tekoa", "of Anathoth" and so on where the KJV has "the Tekoite", "the Antothite".

11:32.t: "Ravines": the KJV's "brooks", meaning valleys that carry water in the rainy season.

11:34.t: Shagee, Sachar, Hagri: the KJV spells them Shage, Sacar and Haggeri. 11:43 Maacah: the KJV's Maachah. 11:44 Jeiel, Hotham: the KJV's Jehiel and Hothan. 11:47 Jaasiel the Mezobaite: the KJV's Jasiel the Mesobaite.

12:3.t: Beracah, Ishmaiah, Jozabad, Isshiah, Azarel: the KJV spells them Berachah, Ismaiah, Josabad, Jesiah and Azareel. "Of Gibeah", "of Anathoth", "of Gibeon", "of Gederah": the KJV's "the Gibeathite", "the Antothite" and so on. Korahites: the KJV's "Korhites".

12:8.t: "Spear": the KJV's "buckler", a small shield; most Hebrew copies read "spear". "Gazelles": the KJV's "roes".

12:14.t: "The least of them was in charge of 100, and the greatest of 1,000": as the KJV reads it. The Hebrew can also mean that the least of them was equal to a hundred men and the greatest to a thousand.

12:15.t: "The first month": Nisan, in March and April, when the Jordan floods with melted snow.

12:18.t: "The Spirit came upon": the Hebrew says the Spirit "clothed" Amasai, as with Gideon (Judges 6:34). The KJV prints "spirit" in lowercase; it is capitalized here as the Spirit of God. "Chief of the officers": the KJV's "chief of the captains"; the Hebrew margin reads "chief of the thirty".

12:19.t: "Rulers": the KJV's "lords", the five rulers of the Philistine cities.

12:21.t: "Bands of raiders": the KJV's "the band of the rovers", the Amalekites who raided Ziklag (1 Samuel 30).

12:29.t: "Remained loyal to": the KJV's "kept the ward of".

12:33.t: "With an undivided heart", "with a whole heart": the KJV's "not of double heart" and "with a perfect heart".

12:38.t: "With an undivided heart", "with a whole heart": the KJV's "not of double heart" and "with a perfect heart".

12:40.t: "Plenty of flour": the KJV lists "meat, meal", where "meat" means food in general.

13:1.t: "Commanders of thousands and of hundreds": the KJV's "captains", army officers over units of a thousand and a hundred men.

15:25.t: "Commanders of thousands and of hundreds": the KJV's "captains", army officers over units of a thousand and a hundred men.

13:3.t: "We did not seek it": the KJV's "we enquired not at it", that is, did not seek God's will at the ark; see darash, 10:13-14.

13:5.t: "The Shihor of Egypt": a stream on Egypt's border, perhaps a branch of the Nile. "Lebo-hamath": the KJV's "the entering of Hemath", which may be a town name; it marks the northern border.

13:6.t: "Enthroned between the cherubim": the KJV's "dwelleth between the cherubims". The cherubim were winged figures on the cover of the ark. "Called by His name": the Hebrew is hard; the KJV's "whose name is called on it" means the ark bore the LORD's name.

13:7.t: Uzzah, Perez-uzzah: the KJV spells them Uzza and Perez-uzza. Perez-uzzah means "outbreak against Uzzah".

13:8.t: Instruments: "lyres" for the KJV's "harps" (Hebrew kinnor), "harps" for the KJV's "psalteries" (nebel), "tambourines" for "timbrels", and "ram's horn" for "cornet" (shofar). These are used the same way throughout Chronicles. "Celebrated": the KJV's "played", meaning played music and danced.

15:16.t: Instruments: "lyres" for the KJV's "harps" (Hebrew kinnor), "harps" for the KJV's "psalteries" (nebel), "tambourines" for "timbrels", and "ram's horn" for "cornet" (shofar). These are used the same way throughout Chronicles. "Celebrated": the KJV's "played", meaning played music and danced.
"To play joyful music loudly": the KJV's "sounding, by lifting up the voice with joy".

13:11.t: "Angry": the KJV's "displeased"; the Hebrew means it burned in him.

14:4.t: Elpelet, Eliphelet: the KJV spells them Elpalet and Eliphalet. The list differs slightly from 3:5-8. Beeliada ("the Lord knows") is called Eliada ("God knows") in 3:8 and 2 Samuel 5:16; see 8:33.

14:10.t: "Asked God": the KJV's "enquired of God", the Hebrew shaal, to ask for an answer.

14:14.t: "Asked God": the KJV's "enquired of God", the Hebrew shaal, to ask for an answer.
"Balsam trees": the KJV's "mulberry trees". The Hebrew word (baka) names a tree whose identity is uncertain.

14:12.t: 2 Samuel 5:21 says David and his men carried off the idols; Chronicles adds that they were burned, as the Law required (Deuteronomy 7:5).

14:16.t: Gezer: the KJV spells it Gazer here.

15:1.t: "Houses": the KJV's word; this probably means a palace with its buildings.

15:13.t: "In the way He has prescribed": the KJV's "after the due order". Moses' Law required the Levites to carry the ark with poles (Numbers 4:15, 7:9), not on a cart.

15:18.t: Eliphelehu: the KJV spells it Elipheleh. "Second rank": the KJV's "second degree".

15:20.t: Alamoth and Sheminith are musical terms whose meaning is uncertain. Alamoth may mean "young women", perhaps a high pitch; Sheminith may mean "the eighth", perhaps an octave lower or an eight-stringed instrument. The KJV's "to excel" means to lead.

15:22.t: Chenaniah: some take the Hebrew to mean he was in charge of carrying the ark rather than of the singing.

15:24.t: Joshaphat, Nethanel: the KJV spells them Jehoshaphat and Nethaneel.

15:27.t: "Ephod": a linen garment worn by priests in worship.

15:29.t: "Leaping and celebrating": the KJV's "dancing and playing".

16:1.t: "Peace offerings": a sacrifice shared in a meal, celebrating fellowship with God (Leviticus 3).

16:3.t: "A flask of wine": as in the KJV, which supplies "wine". The Hebrew word (ashishah) probably means a cake of raisins.

16:4.t: "To call to mind": the KJV's "to record"; the Hebrew means to bring to remembrance, perhaps by praying or singing.

16:5.t: "Jeiel ... and Jeiel": the name appears twice, as in the Hebrew; the first may be Jaaziel (15:18).

16:7.t: "First": the KJV's word; it may mean this was the first time the psalm was used, or that David now first put Asaph in charge.

16:8.t: The psalm is drawn from Psalm 105:1-15, Psalm 96:1-13 and Psalm 106:1, 47-48. It is printed without quotation marks, as a song text, so the words spoken inside it take double quotation marks.

16:12.t: "Rulings": the KJV's "judgments", God's decisions and decrees.

16:24.t: "The nations": the KJV's "the heathen", meaning the non-Israelite peoples, here and elsewhere in Chronicles.

16:29.t: "The beauty of holiness": kept from the KJV. It may also mean "in holy clothing", the festive dress of worship.

16:31.t: "The LORD is King": the KJV's "The LORD reigneth".

16:34.t: "His steadfast love endures forever": the KJV's "his mercy endureth for ever". hesed is loyal, committed love that keeps its promises, especially within a covenant; no single English word covers it, and the KJV uses "mercy", "kindness" and "lovingkindness". See the Original language note on 16:34.

"His steadfast love endures forever" (Hebrew ki le'olam hasdo): the KJV's "his mercy endureth for ever". Hesed is loyal, committed love that keeps its promises, especially within a covenant; no single English word covers it, and the KJV uses "mercy", "kindness" and "lovingkindness" (see Genesis 24:27). This refrain, God's covenant love lasting for all time, runs through Chronicles (2 Chronicles 5:13, 7:3, 7:6, 20:21) and is repeated in every verse of Psalm 136. le'olam means "for a very long time" or "for all time".

16:41.t: "His steadfast love endures forever": the KJV's "his mercy endureth for ever". hesed is loyal, committed love that keeps its promises, especially within a covenant; no single English word covers it, and the KJV uses "mercy", "kindness" and "lovingkindness". See the Original language note on 16:34.
"Chosen and named": the KJV's "expressed by name". "Instruments for the songs of God": the KJV's "musical instruments of God".

"His steadfast love endures forever" (Hebrew ki le'olam hasdo): the KJV's "his mercy endureth for ever". Hesed is loyal, committed love that keeps its promises, especially within a covenant; no single English word covers it, and the KJV uses "mercy", "kindness" and "lovingkindness" (see Genesis 24:27). This refrain, God's covenant love lasting for all time, runs through Chronicles (2 Chronicles 5:13, 7:3, 7:6, 20:21) and is repeated in every verse of Psalm 136. le'olam means "for a very long time" or "for all time".

16:39.t: "High place": a hilltop shrine. Here the tabernacle of Moses stood at Gibeon (21:29, 2 Chronicles 1:3).

17:6.t: "Judges": the leaders of Israel before the kings. 2 Samuel 7:7 reads "tribes".

17:13.t: "I will be his Father": capitalized as God speaking of Himself. Hebrews 1:5 applies this verse to Christ.
"My steadfast love": the KJV's "my mercy". 2 Samuel 7:15 has the same promise.

"My steadfast love" (Hebrew hasdi): hesed is loyal, committed love that keeps its promises, especially within a covenant; no single English word covers it, and the KJV uses "mercy", "kindness" and "lovingkindness" (see Genesis 24:27). Here it is God's covenant love for David's line, promised as a lasting gift. Unlike Saul, David's son may be punished but will not lose God's hesed (2 Samuel 7:14-15).

17:17.t: "As a man of high rank": the Hebrew is difficult; the KJV's "according to the estate of a man of high degree" is followed.

17:21.t: "To make a name for Yourself": the Hebrew switches from "God" to "You" in mid-sentence, as the KJV shows.

17:25.t: "Revealed to": the KJV's "told", literally "uncovered the ear of". "Found courage": the KJV's "found in his heart".

18:1.t: "From the control of": the KJV's "out of the hand of". 2 Samuel 8:1 reads Metheg-ammah.

18:2.t: "Subjects": the KJV's "servants". "Tribute": the KJV's "gifts", payments owed by a conquered people.

18:6.t: "Subjects": the KJV's "servants". "Tribute": the KJV's "gifts", payments owed by a conquered people.
"Gave David victory": the KJV's "preserved David"; the Hebrew means saved or gave victory.

18:13.t: "Subjects": the KJV's "servants". "Tribute": the KJV's "gifts", payments owed by a conquered people.
"Gave David victory": the KJV's "preserved David"; the Hebrew means saved or gave victory.

18:3.t: Hadadezer: the KJV spells it Hadarezer.
"When Hadadezer went": the Hebrew says only "as he went"; it could also mean David.

19:16.t: Hadadezer: the KJV spells it Hadarezer.

18:4.t: "1,000 chariots, 7,000 horsemen": 2 Samuel 8:4 reads 1,700 horsemen. "Hamstrung": the KJV's "houghed", cutting the leg tendons so the horses could not pull chariots.

18:8.t: Tibhath and Cun: 2 Samuel 8:8 has Betah and Berothai. "Bronze": the KJV's "brass". "The bronze Sea": the large basin for washing in the temple court (2 Chronicles 4:2).

18:12.t: Abishai: 2 Samuel 8:13 credits David with this victory, and the title of Psalm 60 credits Joab with 12,000. The commander and his king may both be named for one campaign.

18:16.t: Abimelech and Shavsha: 2 Samuel 8:17 has Ahimelech and Seraiah. "Secretary": the KJV's "scribe", a royal official.

18:17.t: Cherethites and Pelethites: the king's bodyguard, probably Cretan and Philistine soldiers. "The chief officials": 2 Samuel 8:18 says David's sons were priests.

19:4.t: "In the middle at their buttocks": the KJV's "in the midst hard by their buttocks". Cutting off a man's beard and clothing was a public disgrace.

19:6.t: KJV: "a thousand talents of silver". Mesopotamia: the Hebrew is Aram-naharaim, "Aram of the two rivers"; see Genesis 24:10.

19:7.t: "32,000 chariots": 2 Samuel 10:6 reads 33,000 men in all, hired foot soldiers as well as chariots.

19:18.t: "7,000 of their charioteers and 40,000 foot soldiers": 2 Samuel 10:18 reads 700 charioteers and 40,000 horsemen.

20:1.t: "In the spring": the KJV's "after the year was expired", meaning at the turn of the year. Chronicles leaves out the story of David and Bathsheba, which belongs here (2 Samuel 11-12).

20:2.t: KJV: "a talent of gold". "Their king": the Hebrew is malkam, which may also be Milcom, the god of the Ammonites, as the Greek Old Testament reads it.

20:3.t: "Cut them with saws": as in the KJV. The Hebrew may instead mean "set them to work with saws", and 2 Samuel 12:31 reads "put them under saws" in the sense of forced labor. "Iron threshing sledges": the KJV's "harrows of iron".

20:4.t: Sibbecai: the KJV spells it Sibbechai. "The giants": the KJV's "the giant"; the Hebrew is Rapha, the Rephaim, a race of tall people.

20:5.t: Elhanan killed Lahmi the brother of Goliath. 2 Samuel 21:19 reads "Elhanan ... slew the brother of Goliath", the KJV supplying "the brother of" from this verse.

20:7.t: "Taunted": the KJV's "defied". Shimea: 2 Samuel 21:21 spells it Shimeah.

21:1.t: "Satan": the parallel in 2 Samuel 24:1 says that the anger of the LORD "moved David" to count Israel. The Hebrew satan means "adversary, accuser", and here, without the article, may be read as a name or as "an adversary". Readers have long seen the two accounts as describing God's permission and Satan's action in the same event. See the Original language note on 21:1.

"Satan" (Hebrew satan, "adversary, accuser"): in most of the Old Testament the word has the article, "the satan", the accuser (Job 1-2, Zechariah 3:1-2). Here it has no article and may be read as a name, Satan, or as "an adversary". 2 Samuel 24:1 says the LORD's anger moved David; Chronicles names the agent through whom the testing came. Readers have long seen the two accounts as describing God's permission and Satan's action in the same event.

21:3.t: "Bring guilt on": the KJV's "be a cause of trespass to".

21:5.t: 1,100,000 and 470,000: 2 Samuel 24:9 reads 800,000 for Israel and 500,000 for Judah. KJV: "a thousand thousand and an hundred thousand".

21:7.t: The KJV's printed text ends this verse with "concerning this thing", a stray phrase from its italic wording; it is not translated twice.

21:12.t: "Three years of famine": 2 Samuel 24:13 reads seven years. "Plague": the KJV's "pestilence". "Territory": the KJV's "coasts".

21:15.t: Ornan: called Araunah in 2 Samuel 24. "Relented concerning the disaster": the KJV's "repented him of the evil". The Hebrew nacham means to be sorry, grieved or moved to change course, not that God had done wrong; "evil" here means harm. See Genesis 6:6-7.

21:23.t: "Grain offering": the KJV's "meat offering", where "meat" means food; this offering was of grain and flour.

21:25.t: KJV: "six hundred shekels of gold by weight". 2 Samuel 24:24 says David bought the threshing floor and oxen for fifty shekels of silver (about 575 grams); Chronicles may count the whole site.

21:26.t: "Fire": compare Leviticus 9:24 and 2 Chronicles 7:1, where fire from God shows that He accepts the sacrifice.

21:29.t: This explains why David sacrificed in Jerusalem rather than at the tabernacle at Gibeon. The threshing floor became the site of the temple (22:1, 2 Chronicles 3:1).

22:2.t: "Foreigners": the KJV's "strangers", non-Israelites living in the land. "Dressed stone": the KJV's "wrought stones".

22:5.t: "Inexperienced": the KJV's "tender". "Exceedingly magnificent": the KJV's "exceeding magnifical".

22:9.t: Solomon sounds like shalom, "peace", which means wholeness, well-being and rest from enemies, not only the absence of war; see the Original language note on 22:9.

"Solomon" (Hebrew Shelomoh) and "peace" (Hebrew shalom): the name sounds like the word for peace. shalom means wholeness, well-being and rest from enemies, not only the absence of war; see 1 Kings 3:15.

22:12.t: "When He puts you in charge of Israel": the KJV's "give thee charge concerning Israel".

22:14.t: KJV: "an hundred thousand talents of gold, and a thousand thousand talents of silver". These are enormous sums, perhaps meant as round figures for a vast amount. "With great effort": the KJV's "in my trouble"; the Hebrew can also mean "in my poverty", meaning at great personal cost.

23:3.t: "By their polls": the KJV's phrase for counting heads, man by man.

23:4.t: "David said": the KJV places these words, "said David", in verse 5; the speech is marked from verse 4.

23:6.t: "Divisions": the KJV's "courses", groups that served by turns.

23:7.t: Ladan: the KJV spells it Laadan. 23:9 Shelomoth: the KJV's Shelomith, the Hebrew margin's Shelomoth. 23:10-11 Zina is called Zizah in 23:11.

23:13.t: "To consecrate the most holy things": the Hebrew can also mean "to be consecrated as most holy", Aaron himself being set apart.

23:20.t: Micah, Isshiah: the KJV spells them Michah and Jesiah.

23:22.t: "Married them": the KJV's "took them", their cousins, so that the family inheritance stayed in the clan (Numbers 36).

23:24.t: Twenty years: compare thirty years in 23:3 and twenty-five in Numbers 8:24. David lowered the age because the Levites' work changed once the ark had a permanent home.

23:25.t: "He lives in Jerusalem forever": the KJV's "that they may dwell in Jerusalem for ever" takes the people as the subject; the Hebrew verb is singular, so it is better read of the LORD.

23:29.t: "The offerings mixed with oil": the KJV's "that which is fried"; the Hebrew word means mixed or soaked.

23:31.t: "New moons": the first day of each month, marked by special offerings.

24:3.t: "David divided them, both Zadok ... and Ahimelech": the KJV's reading, meaning the priestly families of Zadok and Ahimelech. Many modern Bibles read "with the help of Zadok ... and Ahimelech".

24:5.t: "Officials of God": the KJV's "governors of the house of God", where "the house of" is supplied in italics.

24:6.t: "One family was taken for Eleazar, and then one for Ithamar": the Hebrew repeats "taken" for Eleazar and for Ithamar; the lots apparently alternated between the two families.

24:7.t: These twenty-four divisions of priests served at the temple by turns, a week at a time. The eighth, Abijah, was the division of Zechariah, father of John the Baptist (Luke 1:5).

24:15.t: Happizzez: the KJV's Aphses. 24:16 Jehezkel: the KJV's Jehezekel, the same name as Ezekiel.

24:24.t: Micah: the KJV spells it Michah. 24:26-27 "Beno" may mean "his son" in Hebrew.

24:31.t: "On the same terms as": the KJV's "over against", meaning that oldest and youngest were treated alike.

25:1.t: "Set apart": the KJV's "separated". "Prophesy": here the word is used of inspired singing and music in the temple worship, speaking or singing under God's prompting, not only foretelling the future; see the Original language note on 25:1-3.

"Prophesy" (Hebrew naba): the verb behind navi, "prophet", probably "one who is called" or "one who speaks for another", a person through whom God makes His will known (see 1 Samuel 9:9). Here the word is used of inspired singing and music in the temple worship. It means speaking or singing under God's prompting, not only foretelling the future.

25:2.t: Asharelah: the KJV's Asarelah; called Jesharelah in 25:14.

25:3.t: "Six": five names are listed; the Greek Old Testament adds Shimei (compare 25:17).

25:4.t: The last nine names in this verse, from Hananiah on, can also be read in Hebrew as a short prayer or poem: "Be gracious to me, LORD, be gracious to me; You are my God; I have magnified and lifted up help; sitting in trouble, I have spoken visions in abundance."

25:5.t: "Given through the promises of God to exalt him": the KJV's "in the words of God, to lift up the horn". A horn is a picture of strength and honor; God's promise to raise Heman up was fulfilled in his many children.

25:7.t: "Skilled": the KJV's "cunning", in its old sense of skillful.

25:8.t: "For their duties": the KJV's "ward against ward". "Student": the KJV's "scholar".

25:9.t: Each lot fell to a leader with "his sons and his relatives, twelve", making twenty-four groups of twelve, the 288 of 25:7. Izri (25:11) is Zeri (25:3); Azarel (25:18, the KJV's Azareel) is Uzziel (25:4); Shubael (25:20) is Shebuel (25:4).

26:1.t: Korahites: the KJV's "Korhites". "Asaph": probably Ebiasaph (9:19), since Asaph was a Gershonite.

26:3.t: Eliehoenai, Sachar, Nethanel, Peullethai: the KJV spells them Elioenai, Sacar, Nethaneel and Peulthai.

26:5.t: "God had blessed him": compare 13:14, where God blessed Obed-edom's house while the ark was there.

26:7.t: "Able men": the KJV's "strong men" and "able men for strength".

26:10.t: Shimri: the KJV spells it Simri.

26:12.t: "Had duties just as their relatives did": the KJV's "having wards one against another".

26:15.t: "Storehouse": the KJV leaves the Hebrew untranslated, "the house of Asuppim", meaning the house of stores.

26:17.t: "Storehouse": the KJV leaves the Hebrew untranslated, "the house of Asuppim", meaning the house of stores.

26:16.t: "The road that goes up": the KJV's "the causeway of the going up". "Guard stood next to guard": the KJV's "ward against ward".

26:18.t: "Colonnade": the KJV leaves the Hebrew untranslated, "Parbar". The word is rare and may mean a court or an open building on the west side of the temple.

26:20.t: "Dedicated gifts": the KJV's "dedicated things", gifts set apart for the temple.

26:21.t: Ladan: the KJV spells it Laadan. The Hebrew of this verse is awkward; the KJV's sense is kept.

26:25.t: Shelomoth: the KJV spells it Shelomith; the Hebrew margin reads Shelomoth.

26:29.t: "Duties outside the temple": the KJV's "the outward business".

26:30.t: "West of the Jordan": the KJV's "on this side Jordan westward".

27:1.t: "Came on duty and went off duty": the KJV's "came in and went out", each division serving one month a year.

27:2.t: Most of these commanders appear among David's mighty men in 11:10-47. "Of Tekoa", "of Anathoth", "of Netophah", "of Pirathon": the KJV's "the Tekoite", "the Anetothite", "the Netophathite", "the Pirathonite".

27:5.t: "Jehoiada the chief priest": the KJV's "Benaiah the son of Jehoiada, a chief priest" could refer to either man; Jehoiada is named as a priestly leader in 12:27.

27:11.t: Zerahites: the KJV's "Zarhites", descendants of Judah's son Zerah. 27:12 "A Benjaminite": the KJV's "of the Benjamites".

27:13.t: Zerahites: the KJV's "Zarhites", descendants of Judah's son Zerah. 27:12 "A Benjaminite": the KJV's "of the Benjamites".

27:16.t: Maacah: the KJV's Maachah. 27:22 Azarel: the KJV's Azareel.

27:23.t: "As many as the stars of the sky": the promise to Abraham (Genesis 15:5, 22:17).

27:24.t: "Wrath came upon Israel": see chapter 21. "The records": the KJV's "the account of the chronicles".

27:25.t: Jonathan: the KJV's Jehonathan, a longer form of the same name. "Towers": the KJV's "castles".

27:28.t: "Sycamore-fig trees": the KJV's "sycomore trees", a kind of fig, not the American sycamore. "Western foothills": the KJV's "low plains", the Shephelah between the hill country and the coast.

27:31.t: "Hagrite": the KJV's "Hagerite", one of a people of the desert east of Gilead; see 5:10. "Property": the KJV's "substance".

27:32.t: "Uncle": the Hebrew word can also mean a relative more generally.

27:33.t: "The king's friend": a title for a trusted adviser (2 Samuel 15:37).

28:1.t: "Palace officials": the KJV's "officers"; the Hebrew word often means court officials or eunuchs.

28:2.t: "A footstool for our God": the ark is pictured as the footstool of the LORD who is enthroned above the cherubim.

28:7.t: "Rules", "testimonies", "statutes": words for God's laws, the KJV's "judgments", "testimonies" and "statutes".

29:19.t: "Rules", "testimonies", "statutes": words for God's laws, the KJV's "judgments", "testimonies" and "statutes".
"Palace": the KJV's word; the Hebrew birah means a citadel or great building, here the temple.

28:9.t: "A whole heart": the KJV's "a perfect heart". "He will let you find Him": the KJV's "he will be found of thee". "By the Spirit": the KJV's "by the spirit" may mean the Spirit of God or simply David's own mind; it is capitalized here because 28:19 says the plan came from the LORD.

28:12.t: "A whole heart": the KJV's "a perfect heart". "He will let you find Him": the KJV's "he will be found of thee". "By the Spirit": the KJV's "by the spirit" may mean the Spirit of God or simply David's own mind; it is capitalized here because 28:19 says the plan came from the LORD.

28:11.t: "The atonement cover": the KJV's "the mercy seat", the gold lid of the ark where the blood was sprinkled on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16:14-15). The Hebrew kapporet comes from kipper, "make atonement", to remove guilt and defilement so that the relationship with God is restored; see 6:49.

28:15.t: "Lampstands": the KJV's "candlesticks"; they held oil lamps, not candles.

28:17.t: "Meat forks": the KJV's "fleshhooks", forks for handling sacrificial meat. "Dish": the KJV's "bason".

28:18.t: "The chariot, the cherubim": the cherubim over the ark are pictured as the chariot or throne of God.

28:20.t: "Fail you or abandon you": the KJV's "fail thee, nor forsake thee", the words of Moses to Joshua (Deuteronomy 31:6-8).

29:1.t: "Palace": the KJV's word; the Hebrew birah means a citadel or great building, here the temple.

29:2.t: "With all my resources": the KJV's "with all my might". "Glittering stones": the KJV's "glistering stones"; the Hebrew may mean stones set in mortar or a dark ornamental stone.

29:3.t: "A treasure of my own": the KJV's "mine own proper good", meaning personal wealth.

29:4.t: KJV: "three thousand talents of gold ... seven thousand talents of refined silver". Ophir was a land famous for fine gold, perhaps in Arabia or East Africa.

29:5.t: "Give himself freely": the KJV's "consecrate his service", literally "fill his hand", an idiom for ordaining a priest, here used of giving.

29:7.t: KJV: "five thousand talents and ten thousand drams" of gold, "ten thousand talents" of silver, "eighteen thousand talents" of bronze and "one hundred thousand talents" of iron. "Darics": the KJV's "drams". The daric was a Persian gold coin weighing about 8.4 grams, a sum named in the coin known when Chronicles was written.

29:15.t: "There is no hope of staying": the KJV's "there is none abiding". The Hebrew may also mean "there is no hope".

29:18.t: "This purpose and this desire": the KJV's "the imagination of the thoughts".

29:20.t: "Paid honor to the king": the KJV's "worshipped the LORD, and the king". The same Hebrew word means to bow low, whether before God in worship or before a king in respect.

29:22.t: "A second time": the first is in 23:1; 1 Kings 1:32-40 tells of an earlier, hurried anointing.

29:29.t: "Records": the KJV's "book"; the Hebrew dibre means words, acts or records.

29:30.t: "The events that happened": the KJV's "the times that went over".
